title: Isaiah Shirley Named Semifinalist for William V. Campbell Trophy - NC State University Athletics
content: RALEIGH, N. C. – NC State defensive lineman Isaiah Shirley is one of 206 semifinalists for the 2026 William V. Campbell Trophy ®, college football's premier scholar-athlete award. Celebrating its 37th year, the Campbell Trophy ® recognizes the nation's best football scholar-athlete for combined academic success, football performance, and exemplary leadership.Collectively, this year's 206 semifinalists include 130 team captains, 24 All-Americans, and 114 all-conference selections.Shirley is one of 14 ACC players named a semifinalist for the award. He is majoring in sport management with a minor in psychology, holds a 3.8 GPA, and plans to pursue a postgraduate degree in business finance.Last season, Shirley was named to the All-ACC Academic Football Team and has appeared on the ACC Academic Honor Roll four times. Earlier this year, Shirley was named one of four finalists for the Arthur Ashe Sports Scholars Award. Of 900+ nominees for the award, Shirley was the only football student-athlete named a finalist.Ahead of the 2026 season, his teammates voted him assistant captain. Through three games in 2026, Shirley has totaled seven tackles, including one tackle for a loss. The Wolfpack have appeared in a bowl game every season Shirley has been on the team.Shirley, an active member of the community, has spoken at numerous high schools, sharing his testimony and offering advice grounded in his beliefs. He is involved with Uplifting Athletes, an organization that uses sports to build a community that invests in the lives of people affected by rare diseases.Shirley has already appeared on the Wuerffel Trophy Watch List and the AFCA Good Works Team.The NFF will announce 12 to 16 finalists on October 21. Each finalist will receive an $18, 000 postgraduate scholarship and become a member of the 2026 NFF National Scholar- Athlete Class Presented by Fidelity Investments.The finalists will be recognized at the 68th NFF Annual Awards Dinner, presented by Las Vegas, on December 8 at the Bellagio Resort & Casino in Las Vegas. One finalist will be selected as the recipient of the 37th Campbell Trophy®, with his postgraduate scholarship increased to $25,000.The NFF National Scholar-Athlete Awards, presented by Fidelity Investments, are in their 68th year and have recognized 954 individuals. This year's scholarships will push the program's all-time distribution above $ 13 million.

title: USA v Mexico In Continental Cup - SD Sockers
content: The calendar has turned from summer to fall, and the sights and sounds of the world’s fastest soccer game are about to move from memory to reality once again, as the Continental Cup unofficially kicks off the beginning of the indoor soccer preseason on Saturday night at Frontwave Arena. Team USA takes on Team Mexico for a 7:00pm kickoff, with tickets available at frontwavearena.com. All-Star rosters will take the floor on Saturday night to play for country over club, with stars from the San Diego Sockers and the Major Arena Soccer League going head-to-head in a 60-minute “friendly” match. Players from the Sockers, Empire Strykers, Tacoma Stars, Milwaukee Wave and Lehigh Valley Phantoms will take part in the event, as well as some of Tijuana’s top indoor soccer talent. The San Diego Sockers coaching staff will split up to manage the soccer strategy, as head coach Phil Salvagio will lead Team USA against assistant coach Rene Ortiz’ Team Mexico. “We know the indoor fans have been waiting through the longest offseason in professional sports, but the new season is almost here,” said Salvagio, “Saturday night kicks it off. The talent will be great, and the action will be intense.” Team USA features nine members of the MASL Ron Newman Cup champion San Diego Sockers, including goalkeepers Chris Toth and Boris Pardo, forwards Luiz Morales and Abdul Mansaray, midfielders Andrew Estrella, Sebastian Mendez and Adrian Reyes, and defenders Jesus Pacheco and Drew Ruggles. The Milwaukee Wave, MASL runners-up to the Sockers in 2025-26, are also prominently featured, with MASL Defender of the Year Mario Alvarez and MVP finalist Alex Sanchez both scheduled to play. Empire Strykers star midfielder Justin Stinson and former Sockers forward Nick Perera (who has returned to Tacoma Stars as player/GM) round out the star-studded roster. Team Mexico is led by Sockers captain and All-Star defender Cesar Cerda, and includes fellow Sockers star midfielder Charlie Gonzalez, Sockers defender Luis “Peewee” Ortega, and Empire Strykers keeper Brandon Gomez. The real treat for Sockers fans, however, will be the opportunity to cheer on Tijuana soccer greats such as Brandon Escoto--the reigning TST 7v7 Million Dollar Goal-scorer--along with other former Sockers Christian Gutierrez, Irvin Mojica, Luis Perez, and Ismael Rojo, for rare appearances north of the border. TJ talents Edgar Alvarez, Javier Gallegos, Ramon Ramirez, Jaime Romero, and Rodolfo Valenzuela fill out a Team Mexico side that would be a league favorite if it could roster in the MASL. The Major Arena Soccer League 2026-27 season will kick off on Thanksgiving weekend, as the San Diego Sockers aim to repeat as league champions and capture the 18th title in franchise history. More information on Saturday’s Continental Cup, as well as ticket options, are available by visiting frontwavearena.com. The Cup will be broadcast live on YouTube on the MASL TV channel, with Craig Elsten and Tony Sanchez handling play-by-play and analyst duties.

title: Netherlands v Germany: Klopp and Xavi begin revival projects with derby - The Guardian
content: Jürgen Klopp and Xavi Hernández face each other in Nations League as they take the reins following disappointing World Cups Before the latest instalment of a time-honoured international rivalry gearing up for two distinct new beginnings, Jürgen Klopp could not resist sprinkling a little of the old mischief. “The good thing is that we both have the exact same situation,” he said of Xavi Hernández, his counterpart when Germany visit the Netherlands on Thursday night. “We met on Monday and play on Thursday. And the coach knows the players from television. I actually know more of the Dutch players personally than Xavi does. Whether that’s an advantage, I don’t know, but it’s still a fact.” In his public appearances Klopp has been on irrepressible form since taking the role in July. The task of whipping Germany back into shape has visibly and audibly topped up the energy levels that had drained by the time he departed Liverpool. Klopp, his wit sharp and appetite piqued, looks a far cry from the character who, to most trained eyes, was going through the motions upon his unveiling as Red Bull’s head of global soccer early last year. Securing Klopp was a coup for the German football federation even if it came with a caveat, issued within seconds of his introduction to the media, that he would not be seen for dust if his family were hounded by the media. Xavi’s arrival in Amsterdam is no less fascinating even if, in the Dutch way, no bones were made by his employers about the fact Pep Guardiola and Arne Slot had been higher in their sights after Ronald Koeman’s departure. He is the Netherlands’ first foreign manager since Ernst Happel’s 10-month stint ended in 1978 but the fit is instinctively pleasing. Even if Guardiola was out of reach, they could land upon another product of the Johan Cruyff school that created modern-day Barcelona. If Xavi is to take the Netherlands, occasionally exciting but frequently unstable during a World Cup run that shuddered to a halt in the last 32, back to their roots it will require a measure of patience. The pool of players does not allow much else; the recall of Borussia Dortmund’s Joey Veerman, who has not played international football for more than two years, speaks of the need for a technically adept midfield fulcrum but otherwise Xavi has scant scope for surprises. Virgil van Dijk will continue as captain despite considering international retirement during the summer; the head coach’s options may feel more complete when Frenkie de Jong and Donyell Malen have returned from injury. Xavi has resisted any temptation to engage in analysis of the Netherlands’ performance in the United States. “I don’t talk about the past,” is the standard line, ironically an easier one to roll out if the Nations League opener in Amsterdam brings a performance redolent of headier times. The revolution may have to be conducted with minimal effusive pronouncements from the coach. It is certainly a less dramatic shake-up than the one Klopp, acting like a man licensed to break a few moulds, has enacted before the next fortnight’s four-game baptism. It raised eyebrows when Klopp named a squad of 44 players for the matches against the Netherlands, Serbia and, home and away, Greece. The expanded unit will be split into two: half will play on Thursday and in Germany’s next game, at home against the Greeks, and the remainder will be involved in the second two games. Only Finn Dahmen, the Augsburg goalkeeper, will be required across the set. “I want to get to know as many players as possible,” Klopp said. “There is no A or B team. The squads are put together in a way that makes sense on the pitch and in terms of character and experience.” Club managers feeling squeamish at their players’ workloads during this expanded break will immediately have warmed to Klopp’s split selection. But the priority is to discover who best fits his vision for an intensely committed, front-footed, enthusiastic Nationalmannschaft that places round pegs, even unexpected ones, in round holes. Four players from Freiburg have made his sprawling selection; so has Felix Keidel from promoted Elversberg. Mika Baur of Celtic and the Hoffenheim winger Bambasé Conté were both stunned to receive first call-ups. The Brentford midfielder Vitaly Janelt joins his teammate Kevin Schade in the fray. Sixteen are uncapped. Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Last weekend Klopp and his coaching staff convened at their headquarters in Herzogenaurach to watch as many of their charges’ domestic games as possible in one go. Freiburg’s Max Rosenfelder, one of the new brood, acknowledged the aura surrounding Klopp and described him as “a very, very special person”. Even if the mixed lineups prove to lack experience and cohesion, Klopp hopes his charges’ sheer thirst for the task will lift Germany from the doldrums of their most recent World Cup flop. If he can unite 44 players, why not a whole country? Among Klopp’s many recent pronouncements was the timely intervention in favour of “positive patriotism” that followed an election victory by the anti‑immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party in Saxony‑Anhalt. If it is some time since Germany’s football team have been at their best, perhaps the same may be said for the nation too. In the Dutch capital, two big‑name managers will take their first steps towards bringing the good times back. “It could be a bit wild, but I accept that, it just has to be lively,” Klopp said. That comes with something approaching a cast‑iron guarantee.

title: ACLU-MN, Pro Bono Partners, Responds to Federal Court’s Decision to Dismiss Tincher v. Mullin - ACLU of Minnesota
content: MINNEAPOLIS – On Friday, Sept. 18, a Federal Court dismissed Tincher v. Mullin. This case was brought by the ACLU-MN and pro-bono partners on behalf of protesters, observers, and journalists who were stopped, arrested, brutalized, and detained in the course of exercising their First Amendments Rights during Operation Metro Surge. The ACLU-MN is disappointed in the court’s decision that plaintiffs lack standing to seek injunctive relief, and we will use every tool at our disposal to continue seeking accountability for the plaintiffs and declarants. Tincher v. Mullin (then Tincher v. Noem) was filed by the ACLU-MN and pro bono partners Ciresi Conlin, Forsgren Fisher, and Riach Law on Dec. 17, 2025, as Operation Metro Surge was intensifying. In response to unlawful attacks on their neighbors, community members showed up to observe and protest. Federal agents countered their dissent with intimidation and force clearly intended to interfere with people’s exercise of free speech and their right to peaceably assemble and express disagreement with the government. Susan Tincher, the named plaintiff in Tincher v. Mullin, awoke on Dec. 9 to a notification that an ICE detainment was happening blocks from her house. She quickly drove to the location of the ICE activity and stood on a public street without interfering with the agents. When Tincher asked, “are you ICE,” agents grabbed her, slammed her face-first into the snow and detained her. She was brought to the Whipple Federal building where agents cut off her wedding ring and some of her clothing. Hours after being detained, Tincher was released without charges or an explanation for her arrest. Tincher’s story is just one of the hundreds that the ACLU-MN received from Minnesotans during Operation Metro Surge. And, while the government declared an end to the operation, we continue to receive reports of federal agents arresting and detaining our neighbors violating Minnesotan’s rights. “We are reviewing this decision and assessing our next steps,” said Teresa Nelson, ACLU-MN Legal Director. “The plaintiffs and declarants in Tincher v. Mullin were gravely harmed by federal immigration enforcement, and they came forward to tell their stories — despite the federal government's attempts to silence their dissent. We will not stop fighting for them, and for everyone harmed by Operation Metro Surge, until the government answers for its violent, unconstitutional assault on Minnesotans. This fight is not over.” The ACLU-MN has filed more than fifteen notices under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) seeking accountability and damages on behalf of individuals harmed by federal agents during Operation Metro Surge, including plaintiffs and declarants in Tincher v. Mullin. “The Federal Tort Claims Act cannot prevent future harm, but it does provide a pathway for individuals to sue the federal government for harms that have already occurred,” said ACLU-MN Deputy Legal Director Catherine Ahlin-Halverson. “It is an imperfect tool, but we are prepared to use every avenue available to demand accountability for what our neighbors experienced.” Sign up to be the first to hear about how to take action. title: Spain v Kazakhstan: how the tie was won - Billie Jean King Cup
content: The 2026 Billie Jean King Cup by Gainbridge Finals continued in Shenzhen with a gripping, compelling and at times crackers quarter-final, which eventually saw Spain shrug off a dogged Kazakhstan. All the headlines will read that Spain have made generational history by reaching their first Billie Jean King Cup semi-final since 2008 – their oldest player, Sara Sorribes Tormo, was just 11 years of age when Spain were last in the semis. Sorribes Tormo and Cristina Bucsa were the Spanish heroines after navigating a rollercoaster encounter with Anna Danilina and Zhibek Kulambayeva, which lasted just over two hours. MORE: Kazakhstan vs Spain report | All you need to know about 2026 BJK Cup Finals With the hand of history firmly on their shoulder, Kazakhstan will be kicking themselves for allowing a host of break points in the deciding doubles to slip through their grasp. Had those break points been seized, Kazakhstan may well have reached their maiden Billie Jean King Cup semi-final, and it would have been achieved without world No. 1 Elena Rybakina. Defeat can be harsh. But, when all is said and done, this tie epitomised what the Billie Jean King Cup – the largest annual women’s international team competition in sport – is all about. It was impossible to take your eyes off the action. It was a cocktail infused with sublimity and ridiculousness. Here's what happened: Spain plotted a course to victory and were set on their way by Jessica Bouzas Maneiro as she defeated 20-year-old Sonja Zhiyenbayeva in the tie’s opening singles match. Bouzas Maneiro, who turns 24 on Thursday and can celebrate her birthday buoyed by victory in national team colours, prevailed 6-2 6-2 in just 62 minutes to fire Spain into a 1-0 lead. As always in the Billie Jean King Cup, the opening singles match does not determine the tie’s outcome, but it can serve as the launchpad for ultimate victory. This was Bouzas Maneiro’s first match-win at a Finals and very much a case of job done. It will have been especially pleasing given there was real pressure and expectation on her shoulders. Indeed, Bouzas Maneiro has struggled in recent months and has not won back-to-back matches since reaching the third round at Wimbledon. The team environment can often have a liberating effect, and Bouzas Maneiro will no doubt take plenty of confidence from this victory to use as fuel for a repeat performance later this week. From here, and in the absence of three-time Grand Slam champion Rybakina, Kazakhstan needed a saviour and found one in the shape of Yulia Putintseva, who hauled her nation level with victory in the second singles match. World No. 79 Putintseva defeated Bucsa 6-2 3-6 6-1 to record her 28th win in the competition, drawing level with all-time Kazakhstan record holder, Galina Voskoboeva. There was impressive court coverage and craft by both players during a match that went the distance, with Bucsa attempting to post her first victory from a set down since January – and opportunity knocked at the door. Bucsa was leading 40-15 in the fourth game of the third set, but Putintseva was far from done. The 31-year-old – always a bundle of energy – was relentless and fought back to take that game and lead 3-1. From there, she never looked back. Bear in mind that had Bucsa won that set, the tie would have been done and dusted. Putintseva’s intervention – sealed with a lovely cross-court drop shot – was timely to say the least. Her efforts ensured the tie was decided on the doubles, and the encounter did not disappoint, as Olympic bronze medallists Sorribes Tormo and Bucsa united to great effect once again. The Spaniards cantered to the first set to put their nation on the brink of victory before the second set unfolded in dramatic fashion. It could have gone either way, but Sorribes Tormo and Bucsa found a way to win 6-2 7-5 – more on that to come. While ultimately in vain, the singles victory for Putintseva was a great moment in this tie. Sometimes the treasure is not always at the surface – and the storyline in the Billie Jean King Cup is not always the result. Indeed, not only did Putintseva’s defeat of Bucsa breathe new life into Kazakhstan’s quest to reach the semi-finals by levelling the tie at 1-1, but there was also a wider, personal significance. Putintseva endured a torrid time at Shenzhen Bay Sports Centre at the 2025 Finals. Firstly, she failed to convert two match points during a third-set tie-break with Emma Navarro in the opening singles match of Kazakhstan’s quarter-final with the United States. She then returned for the winner-takes-all doubles, only for her and Rybakina to lose another tie-break, against Jessica Pegula and Taylor Townsend, which ultimately ushered in an early exit. Her win this time around was a matter of personal redemption and her celebration reflected that. There were important twists within the match – as there are in any encounter – but Putintseva’s was a classic Billie Jean King Cup moment of vindication. There were a few. Kazakhstan had huge momentum following Putintseva’s victory. Bucsa looked fatigued at the end of that contest, but she picked herself up to partner Sorribes Tormo to success in the doubles. In many respects, this is a fire and ice combination. Sorribes Tormo certainly brought much-needed energy to proceedings, and she and Bucsa were 3-0 up in the blink of an eye to immediately deflate the Kazakhstani bubble following Putintseva’s triumph. Nobody is naïve enough to think a match is done and dusted within the opening three games, and Danilina and Kulambayeva certainly had their moments, putting their opponents under pressure. However, in the opening set, that three-game burst by Sorribes Tormo and Bucsa set the tone, lay down a marker, calmed any lingering nerves and reinstated belief. Then came the craziness and perhaps where the third match of this tie was ultimately won and lost. Danilina and Kulambayeva had break points to go 3-0, 4-3, 5-4 and 6-5 up in the second set, but lost all four games in question. During those four games, each time Sorribes Tormo and Bucsa faced a break of serve, they managed to conjure an escape route. As the saying goes, it is not necessarily how many points you win, but whether you win the important ones. The scoreboard in that final match read 6-2 7-5 to Sorribes Tormo and Bucsa – nothing out of the ordinary there – but one statistic painted a bigger picture. Danilina and Kulambayeva simply did not take the chances they carved out and converted just two of the 20 break points which came their way. Sorribes Tormo and Bucsa, meanwhile, converted five of eight. Carla Suarez Navarro (Spain captain): “Reaching the semi-finals is so important. It is something that we have always tried to do. It is something we have not done for a long time because this competition is so difficult and every tie is so difficult. “Our moment is now? We won today and we can still dream of our goal to win Billie Jean King Cup. For us, the Spanish people and the Spanish tennis federation, this is an important achievement.” Bucsa: “I try to put in all my effort. I gave everything I had in the singles match. Then in the doubles, all the crowd and my team, they supported me so much. I gave my last drop of energy. I am so happy to win.” Putintseva: “I wasn’t even worried because every time I play, I end up playing three sets, even though I don’t want to. It always seems to happen the same way. “In the third set I was very focused not to do any mistakes. I thought if she wants to win this match, she must hit winners and hit winners not in the first two shots because I am going to run and get everything back. Then we will see what can happen.” Bouzas Maneiro: “Billie Jean King Cup is super special. We have good relationships in the team and good communication. From my side, I have everything with my team and all that I need in every moment. They understand me and they have a lot of empathy.” Spain secured their place in the last four of the Billie Jean King Cup and will now face Czechia – conquerors of Great Britain on Tuesday – for a place in the final. That showdown will take place on Friday. Whoever wins that tie can take a breath on Saturday – the day of the second semi-final – and ensure that preparations are completely on point for what promises to be a titanic clash. For now, however, Spain can revel in reaching the semi-finals of this competition for the first time in 18 years.

title: The People v. Gorilla Grodd Takes Place After "Man of Tomorrow": Gunn - Bleeding Cool News
content: Posted in: HBO, Max, Movies, TV | Tagged: The People v. Gorilla Grodd James Gunn clarified where on the DCU timeline The People v. Gorilla Grodd takes place, and the earliest it could possibly premiere. Last week, series star Skyler Gisondo (Jimmy Olsen) shared that he believed that DC Studios and Warner Bros. Television's The People v. Gorilla Grodd, stemming from Tony Yacenda and Dan Perrault, would be set between Superman and Supergirl, and the upcoming Man of Tomorrow. In his defense, he wasn't offering that intel as gospel set in stone. Thankfully, Gunn offered a bit of clarity on the matter, noting that the streaming series takes place after Man of Tomorrow. In addition, The People v. Gorilla Grodd won't be released before the upcoming film, which would mean the latter half of 2027, at the earliest. Here's a look at what Gunn had to share regarding the upcoming series's place on the DCU timeline and when it will be released: A superintelligent ape is convicted of murdering his father, the King of Gorilla City. In an eight-part "true" crime docuseries, the Daily Planet's Jimmy Olsen reopens the case, investigating whether Gorilla Grodd was wrongly convicted in one of Metropolis' most famous murder trials. The streaming series stars Skyler Gisondo as Jimmy Olsen, Jimmy Tatro as Gorilla Grodd, Beck Bennett as Steve Lombard, Mikaela Hoover as Cat Grant, and Wendell Pierce as Perry White. Additional cast includes Mary Holland, Eduardo Franco, Arian Moayed, Dan Perrault, Andrew Leeds, and Tim Baltz. James Gunn and Peter Safran, executive producers and DC Studios' Co-Chairmen & Co-CEOs, shared, "Between Skyler's wonderful performance and the fantastic chemistry of the Daily Planet cast, we knew coming out of 'Superman' that this would be a fun world to explore. We're excited to work with the brilliant Dan Perrault and Tony Yacenda to take the audience down some of the darker and funnier streets and alleyways of the DCU as Jimmy spotlights the Metropolis criminal justice system for his docuseries." "We're excited by the challenge of creating a series that feels less like an entry into the DCU and more like an artifact from it. A Daily Planet original documentary made for the people of Metropolis. We hope it'll appeal to fans of the comics, comedy and true crime. And while we can't speak for audiences here yet, we already know it's a huge hit in Metropolis. They love this series," Tony Yacenda and Perrault added. Stemming from DC Studios in association with Warner Bros. Television, The People v. Gorilla Grodd is executive produced by James Gunn, Peter Safran, Tony Yacenda, and Dan Perrault. Yacenda and Perrault also serve as showrunners and writers, with all episodes directed by Yacenda.

title: This GTA V mod lets you destroy Flock cameras. Its creator explains why. - Mashable
content: Los Santos has a new way to get you in trouble, and you don’t even have to commit a crime. A new Grand Theft Auto V mod from artist Morry Kolman, who goes by WTTDOTM online, installs 235 virtual Flock license plate reader cameras around the game’s fictional city. Called Grand Theft Automated License Plate Reader, or GTALPR, it brings an extra layer of surveillance to your next drive. And because this is GTA, you can destroy the cameras and collect in-game cash from their wreckage. But the opportunity to blow them up is only part of the point. Kolman wants players to feel what happens when a familiar environment becomes a place where they’re constantly being watched. "I’m an artist, and much of my practice is based around giving people interesting and engaging ways to learn about the technological and political world around them," Kolman told Mashable. "GTALPR is very much in that vein." For Kolman, a game modeled on an American city, and familiar to millions of players, offered a way to make surveillance tangible. "Suddenly, you're always watched," he added. "With the simple addition of some cameras, the entire environment gains a new passive layer of hostility." In the real world, Flock’s automated license plate readers capture vehicle images and enable police to search for vehicles and receive alerts about those on watchlists. Flock pitches the technology as a way to help law enforcement locate wanted vehicles. Civil liberties groups, including the ACLU, argue that these networks enable mass surveillance of people going about their everyday lives. Kolman’s virtual version draws directly from the geography of the real network. "I chose 235 for the number of cameras to use in GTALPR because it is 1/10th the amount of Flock cameras currently in LA County, and Los Santos is about 1/10th its real counterparts size," he told Mashable. His project page identifies the community mapping project DeFlock as the source for the camera count. The placements aren’t random, either. Kolman built himself a tool to compare the real and fictional maps, then used it to place cameras in corresponding locations. "The closest comparison is probably the area around Santa Monica Pier vs. Del Perro Pier," he said. The result brings a real-world surveillance footprint into a place players may already know street by street. One of the mod’s most pointed feature kicks in when players haven’t committed a crime. Each time a player passes through a camera’s field of view, there’s a 1-in-20 chance it will trigger an unprovoked police chase to "represent this pattern of false reports, and show that living with this surveillance is not a matter of 'having nothing to hide'... it is simply a matter of 'when will it happen to you,'" Kolman described. His broader argument is that avoiding wrongdoing doesn’t eliminate the risks of being surveilled. He described the mechanic as a challenge to the familiar reassurance that people with "nothing to hide" have nothing to worry about. Players can also dismantle the virtual network. Destroy a camera and collect its remains, and the mod awards $600 in game currency. The reward price is based on the estimated value of the parts inside a real Flock camera, after the group Eyes Off Cedar Rapids took one apart to examine its hardware. There’s also built-in speedrun tracking for destroying the cameras, plus an option to render and save the images they capture — including pictures of players destroying them. It’s an absurd addition to a game already full of opportunities for mayhem, but a fitting one in a country where Flock cameras have made everyday drives part of a searchable surveillance network. As Kolman puts it, "I put Flock cameras in GTA V as a way to highlight and make tangible the pervasive intrusion of Flock and other ALPR cameras into daily American life via a game that is based on an American city and that millions of my fellow citizens are intimately familiar with." The mod and its installation instructions are available through Kolman’s website. Olivia Tauber is the deputy editor of digital culture, covering creators, media, movies, beauty, and more. She holds a Master's degree in Journalism from NYU and a Bachelor's from the University of Michigan. She also runs Fan Mail, a weekly pop-culture newsletter.

title: IKEA v Vlaams Belang: free speech sold separately? - Inventa
content: Political parties often borrow the familiarity of well-known trademarks to make a message more recognisable. But when does that use fall under freedom of expression, and when does it amount to taking unfair advantage of another's reputation? In Inter IKEA Systems v Vlaams Belang (C‑298/23), delivered on 8 September 2026, the CJEU set out the criteria for assessing "due cause" in the use of marks with a reputation for political parody. Vítor Palmela Fidalgo shares his initial takeaways on the ruling, examining how due cause is taking on the function of a fair use clause and why the room the Court appears to leave for political speech may in practice be narrower than its reasoning suggests. title: Smith Named Semifinalist for William V. Campbell Trophy - Arkansas Razorbacks
content: FAYETTEVILLE, Ark. – The National Football Foundation and College Hall of Fame (NFF) named Arkansas running back Sutton Smith as a semifinalist for the 2026 William V. Campbell Trophy, the organization announced Wednesday. The Campbell Trophy® recognizes an individual as the best football scholar-athlete in the nation for his combined academic success, football performance and exemplary leadership. The semifinalist selection marks Smith’s first in his collegiate career. The Marietta, Ga., product has rushed for 1,182 total yards and 12 touchdowns on 225 carries while averaging 5.3 yards per attempt during his five-year college career. He’s also registered 50 receptions for 381 yards receiving while tallying 867 total return yards on 46 returns. Nominated by their schools, which are limited to one nominee each, each candidate must be competing in the 2026 season as a senior in his final year of eligibility or a graduate student/graduate transfer who has already earned a degree; have a cumulative undergraduate GPA of at least 3.2 on a 4.0 scale; have outstanding football ability as a first team player or significant contributor; and have demonstrated strong leadership and citizenship. The class is selected each year by the NFF Awards Committee, which is composed of a nationally recognized group of media, NFF College Football Hall of Famers and athletics administrators. Smith was one of 14 student-athletes from the SEC on the record-breaking list of 206 national semifinalists. The NFF will announce 12 to 16 finalists on Oct. 21, and each of them will receive an $18,000 postgraduate scholarship as a member of the 2026 NFF National Scholar-Athlete Class Presented by Fidelity Investments. The finalists will travel to the Bellagio Resort & Casino in Las Vegas for the 68th NFF Annual Awards Dinner Presented by Las Vegas on Dec. 8, where their accomplishments will be highlighted in front of one of the most powerful audiences in all of sports. During the event, one member of the class will be declared as the winner of the 37th Campbell Trophy® and have his postgraduate scholarship increased to $25,000. Click here for more information on the Awards Dinner, including options to purchase tickets online, special travel rates to the event from Delta Air Lines and room rates at the Bellagio. Arkansas closes out the non-conference portion of its 2026 schedule against Tulsa, riding a 19-game win streak against the Golden Hurricane dating back to 1977. title: Bentley’s First EV Has 76 Crystals in Its Nose and Super-Fast Charging - MotorTrend
content:
Bentley’s first EV uses crystals and drumbeats to stun the senses. We tend to think of battery electric vehicles as cutting-edge and high-tech—and they are—but how do you blend those aspects with the old-world craftsmanship that’s the hallmark of a Bentley? How does the 2028 Bentley Torcal welcome in this new era while still staying true to the automaker’s 107 years of history? Same way it always has, turns out: with fastidious attention to detail and keeping the human touches front and center. After all, if it’s to achieve the marque’s own goal of becoming the next best Bentley, then the Torcal better come out swinging. Bentley’s decision to totally electrify an SUV first makes sense, as Bentley Bentaygas apparently account for 45 percent of sales. We went in expecting the Torcal to simply be an electric Bentayga, but it’s definitely not just that. To start, it’s lower and shorter than that SUV. The EXP 15 concept’s influence is obvious, especially in the upright front fascia. Four vertical lights inspired by the Bentley Continental T make up the new signature, and this is the first model to employ Bentley’s new winged logo. You’d have to be a real Bentley afficionado to spot the difference, though. The drag coefficient, we’re told, is 0.279. Get used to this look, because it’s the new face of Bentley moving forward. Not just for EVs, but all models. By now, you’ve noticed the sparkles. Bentley said because the electric powertrain doesn’t require a traditional radiator, that freed designers to experiment with something new. What we get is a nose full of literal cut crystals—76 of them, in fact, in three sizes and sourced from local crystal-maker Cumbria. These all sit behind a single plane of composite, the same plastic used in headlights. Upon unlocking the car, a welcome sequence sends beams of light ricocheting over the glass for a dazzling display. We don’t know what repairing or replacing the crystals will look like should you get into a fender-bender, so be careful. Skating backward from the nose, across the beltline, and stopping at the C-pillar is the “endless bonnet” strip of metal trim that comes in either black or silver. It highlights the Torcal’s sizable rear haunches. At the back, the crystal motif continues in the thin taillights, which also wear the diamond-shaped faceting within. There’s a traditional trunk, of course, but also a front trunk that could fit a small carry-on suitcase. Two new colors, Electrum Satin and Astral, also make their debut. Step inside to be greeted by familiar Bentley fare. Rich leathers and quality materials abound. The leather diamond-shaped quilting can now wear various perforation sizes, as Bentley has introduced a new tool for this. Optionally, a new engineered multicolored walnut veneer can feature up to 1,000 layers of pressed wood for an incredibly textured effect. There’s also the option of a triple-striped aluminum. Finally, Merino wool provides the newest upholstery option. It’s not a blend but 100 percent the real stuff, sourced from Fox Brothers in the U.K., who up until now had only crafted the material for suits. The seats, at least in the very brief time we experienced them, remain comfortable and supportive. The rear seat is indeed spacious and doesn’t make you feel like you’re sitting atop a stack of battery cells, as you often do in other EVs. The new curved central screen is where the Torcal loses the plot a bit. True, it’s incredibly high-resolution, neat to look at, and responsive to use. Bentley also claims it ensured a good balance between physical buttons and touchscreen controls. But the lovely climate adjuster “organ stops” with their superlative tactile feedback are gone. In their place are vents you direct via the screen, something we’re never a fan of. A switchable glass roof is a fun touch, but it’s the only roof available, and changing the pattern or opacity requires another visit to a touchscreen menu. Other tech includes power doors all around, as well as facial recognition capabilities and an augmented reality head-up display. There’s an Easter egg hidden in the driver screen startup animation where footage of a real hand delivering a shining glass appears every other few dozen startups, so you never know when you’ll see it next. Optional audio equipment brings 28 speakers, including seat tweeters and headrest speakers, with Dolby Atmos that’ll generate 1,780 watts of sound You’ll also notice a lack of a passenger screen. This, according to Bentley, was a conscious decision, as it doesn’t see it as a value add. Bentley’s definitely onto something there, because apparently the automakers that do offer the screen are finding no one uses it. Sound is and always has been important to the Bentley experience. An EV, obviously, has no sound, so Bentley went out of its way to record a whole album from real-world noises for it. It recorded the sound of a leather hammer tapping on the material for the turn signals, for example, and the digital assistant sound was created by a glass harp. You know Gracie Hart’s talent in Miss Congeniality? It’s that sound. The entry sound was crafted by birdsong. For the sound of driving, Bentley didn’t just tape the sound of a V-8 and send it as is. Inspired by the thrums of the 6.75-liter V-8, it had drummers re-create the rhythm. That’s what you hear both inside and outside the car, and the sound is linked to a torque sensor, so it responds to the physics of motion rather than throttle position. The faster the car moves, the quicker the drumbeats are. The sound is off by default when the car is in Comfort mode, on in Bentley and Refresh modes, and loudest in Sport mode. But if a customer finds it displeasing, it can be shut off regardless of mode. The Torcal is based on the Porsche Cayenne PP41 EV platform, with bodies coming from Volkswagen’s Zwickau plant in Germany. Two models will be offered to start, the base Core version (810 hp and 881 lb-ft of torque) and the S First Edition (876 hp and 996 lb-ft of torque) though both will utilize the 113-kWh battery pack and all-new electrical 800-volt architecture. Bentley says the battery will retain 90 percent of its charge after eight years and 100,000 cycles. Acceleration to 60 is an estimated 3.4 seconds in the Core model and 2.9 seconds in the S First Edition. According to the optimistic WLTP estimate, the Torcal will return 375 miles of range, and the battery can charge from 10 to 80 percent in 16 minutes at a 400-kW fast charger. It has a towing capacity of just under 6,000 pounds. In place of anti-roll bars, the Torcal rides on advanced, adaptive two-valve dampers that can raise and lower independently, resulting in what is surely a phenomenal ride. We certainly thought so in a brief first ride of a prototype model. The driver will be able to select from four driving and chassis modes (Comfort, Refresh, Bentley, and Sport), and each one is distinct. Rear-wheel steering of up to 7 degrees is standard, and hands-free driving will be offered in certain markets. The Torcal will be built in Crewe, England, in a new, state-of-the-art factory Bentley spent billions of pounds revamping. The space was previously used to house spare parts and was once used to build the Rolls-Royce Merlin V-12 engines used in British fighter planes during WWII. It has never been used to build vehicles until now. The Torcal will be painted at a similarly new and state-of-the-art paint shop that’s more advanced and efficient. Unlike the Bentayga, the Torcal is not built to support a hybrid platform. It will only ever be an EV; interestingly, though, Bentley CEO Frank-Steffen Walliser said if the SUV had a V-8, it would look exactly the same. It’s philosophy is, therefore, vehicle first and propulsion method second. On this front, Walliser is also unconcerned about competition coming from the Chinese luxury brands. In his eyes, the Chinese market produces tech-rich and fast cars, not luxury cars. Nothing like a Bentley. “We will not give up on China,” he told MotorTrend, despite a steadily declining year-over-year market share there. But in poking and prodding around the Torcal, we can tell—at least on this first pass—that it wears every bit the same wealth of materials as the Bentleys that have come before it. New and pioneering automakers like Lucid, Rivian, and Tesla aren’t beholden to a past. Bentley is, and even though the Torcal lacks cylinders, it maintains the craftsmanship. All’s left now is to drive it. Pricing will be announced at a later date. Orders open late September, and the first models ship in Q2 of 2027. 810-876-hp/881-996-lb-ft AC DC permanent-magnet electric Get the newest car reviews, hottest auto news, and expert analysis of the latest trends delivered straight to your inbox! I got into cars the way most people do: my dad. Since I was little, it was always something we’d talk about and I think he was stoked to have his kid share his interest. He’d buy me the books, magazines, calendars, and diecast models—everything he could do to encourage a young enthusiast. 

Eventually, I went to school and got to the point where people start asking you what you want to do with your life. Seeing as cars are what I love and writing is what I enjoy doing, combining the two was the logical next step. This dream job is the only one I’ve ever wanted. 

Since then, I’ve worked at Road & Track, Jalopnik, Business Insider, The Drive, and now MotorTrend, and made appearances on Jay Leno’s Garage, Good Morning America, The Smoking Tire Podcast, Fusion’s Car vs. America, the Ask a Clean Person podcast, and MotorTrend’s Shift Talkers. 

In my spare time, I enjoy reading, cooking, and watching the Fast & Furious movies on repeat. Tokyo Drift is the best one. Subscribe to our newsletters to get the latest in car news and have editor curated stories sent directly to your inbox.

title: California Supreme Court to rule Thursday in Bonta v. Bianco ballot seizure case - KESQ
content:
SAN FRANCISCO, Calif. (KESQ) The California Supreme Court will release its decision Thursday in Attorney General Rob Bonta's case against Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco over his seizure of ballots cast by Riverside County voters in the November 2025 Proposition 50 special election. The court posted a notice Wednesday morning saying the opinion in Bonta v. Bianco will be filed at 10 a.m. Thursday, Sept. 24. The case centers on whether Bianco can restart his investigation into the special election. The ruling could also set the rules for how far any California sheriff can go in taking ballots from elections officials. Bianco's deputies seized the ballots from the Riverside County Registrar of Voters under three search warrants served between February and March. The sheriff said he was investigating claims from a local citizens group that the number of votes counted didn't match poll worker records. County officials dispute the group's math. Bonta ordered Bianco to stand down, arguing the sheriff overstepped his authority. On April 8, the Supreme Court took the case, ordered Bianco to pause his investigation and required him to preserve everything he seized. The Sheriff's Office told News Channel 3 in June it still has the ballots. The justices heard the case Aug. 24 at a special session in San Francisco, back to back with Cervantes v. Bianco, a companion case from four Riverside County voters who want the ballots returned to the registrar. The central question is how much power the attorney general holds over an elected county sheriff. The state constitution gives the attorney general direct supervision over every sheriff in California. Bianco argues the attorney general can't shut down a criminal investigation a judge approved. The court also asked both sides to address Senate Bill 73, a new state law signed in May that restricts law enforcement from taking ballots from elections officials. A Supreme Court decision doesn't become final for 30 days. During that time, either side can ask the court to rehear the case. The court's notice does not say whether the voters' case, Cervantes v. Bianco, will be decided at the same time. News Channel 3 will post the ruling and reaction from Bonta and Bianco as soon as it's released. title: Andrew Miller Named Semifinalist for Prestigious 2026 William V. Campbell Trophy® - Harding University Athletics
content: SEARCY — Harding University senior fullback Andrew Miller has been named a semifinalist for the 2026 William V. Campbell Trophy®, the National Football Foundation & College Hall of Fame (NFF) announced Wednesday. Recognized as college football's premier scholar-athlete award and commonly known as the "Academic Heisman," the Campbell Trophy® celebrates its 37th year honoring the nation's absolute best football scholar-athlete for combined academic success, football performance, and exemplary leadership. Miller is one of a record 206 semifinalists across all divisions of college football (FBS, FCS, Division II, Division III, and NAIA), surpassing the previous record of 204 nominees set in 2024. He is one of just 19 student-athletes selected from NCAA Division II and one of only two nominees from the Great American Conference. To be nominated by their respective institutions—which are permitted only one candidate each—student-athletes must be in their final year of eligibility or pursuing graduate study, maintain a cumulative grade-point average of at least 3.20 on a 4.0 scale, possess outstanding football ability as a starter or significant contributor, and demonstrate exemplary leadership and citizenship. A kinesiology major and returning First-Team College Sports Communicators (CSC) Academic All-American, Miller exemplifies the balance of athletic and academic excellence. The Searcy, Arkansas native currently anchors the backfield for the second-ranked Bisons (3-0), leading an offense that ranks No. 1 nationally in rushing (457.0 yards per game). Miller enters Week 4 as the active leader in NCAA Division II in career rushing yards (3,962), rushing touchdowns (55), total touchdowns (55), points scored (330), and yards per carry average (7.3). Across all NCAA divisions (FBS, FCS, D-II, and D-III), Miller ranks second among active players in career rushing yards and rushing touchdowns. Last fall, Miller finished as the national runner-up for the Harlon Hill Trophy, captured the Darren McFadden Award as the top collegiate player in Arkansas, and earned consensus First-Team All-America honors after rushing for a school-record 2,048 yards and 28 touchdowns to lead Harding to an appearance in the NCAA Division II National Championship game. "Every year, I'm amazed by what these young men are able to accomplish," said NFF Chairman Archie Manning, whose sons Peyton (Campbell Trophy® winner) and Eli were named NFF National Scholar-Athletes in 1997 and 2003, respectively. "Playing college football takes an enormous commitment, and to perform at a high level on the field while also excelling in the classroom and serving as a leader on campus is something special. These 206 semifinalists have a lot to be proud of, and it's a privilege to recognize their accomplishments." Collectively, this year's 206 semifinalists hold an average GPA of 3.64 and feature 130 team captains, 24 All-Americans, 20 Academic All-Americans, and 98 players who have already earned their undergraduate degrees. "These 206 semifinalists represent the power of football to develop leaders well beyond the field," said NFF President & CEO Steve Hatchell. "The game challenges young men to compete, lead and pursue excellence, and these candidates have embraced those values in the classroom, on the field and in their communities. They exemplify the kind of leaders the NFF has sought to recognize and develop throughout its history." The NFF will announce 12 to 16 finalists on Wednesday, Oct. 21. Each finalist will receive an $18,000 postgraduate scholarship as a member of the 2026 NFF National Scholar-Athlete Class Presented by Fidelity Investments. The finalists will travel to the Bellagio Resort & Casino in Las Vegas for the 68th NFF Annual Awards Dinner on Dec. 8, where one finalist will be declared the winner of the 37th Campbell Trophy® and have his postgraduate scholarship elevated to $25,000. Miller and the consensus No. 2-ranked Bisons travel to Arkadelphia, Arkansas, this Saturday, Sept. 26, to take on Great American Conference rival Ouachita Baptist at Cliff Harris Stadium. title: Where to Watch: Netherlands v Germany - Four Liverpool Stars Set To Feature & Klopp's Return as Head Coach - Yahoo Sports
content: A fixture that already makes headlines has even more eyes on it this time as two giant European nations go head-to-head in their opening Nations League clashes of the campaign. Both sides will have high aspirations for this tournament, with many eyes being on Liverpool's star players who are all likely to feature in this game, including Virgil van Dijk, Jeremie Frimpong, Cody Gakpo and Ryan Gravenberch. But Florian Wirtz will not feature due to the new German manager Jurgen Klopp naming two separate squads, with Liverpool's number seven set to feature in the second half of the international break. The last time these two nations played each other was during the last Nations League tournament back in 2024, where Germany won in a narrow 1-0 victory in Munich. It was a game that saw Virgil Van Dijk miss out, Florian Wirtz be subbed at half time, and Jeremie Frimpong come off the bench. But now that both sides are under new management, how different will the teams look, and what will differ, if anything, in the result? Both the Netherlands and Germany had disappointing World Cup campaigns, with the Dutch being knocked out in the round of 32 by Morocco on penalties. Germany also exited the tournament at this stage, losing to Paraguay on penalties in what was one of the biggest upsets of the entire competition. Since then, both nations have opted to change managers, with both Ronald Koeman and Julian Nagelsmann being relieved of their duties, and high-profile coaches Xavi and Jurgen Klopp coming in for the Dutch and Germans, respectively. This will be their first game in charge, and both will be looking to get off to a winning start and put a statement out to the rest of the world that they are a team to be feared ahead of Euro 2028, a tournament particularly important for Germany, given they are the host nation. When Jurgen Klopp was announced as German manager, this was seen as a massive move by the German Football Federation. By appointing someone like Klopp, they would need to give him full freedom to do what he needed and wanted in order for this partnership to work, which, historically, FA's don't like to do. But due to the prestige that surrounds the German coach, exceptions were made, and the former Reds boss has been given complete control, and the changes he has implemented are radical. According to BILD, Klopp has reportedly made the following adjustments to how the national team will run: Players must arrive together and on time for scheduled team dinners No phones are allowed before matches, with Klopp demanding complete focus and concentration on the task at hand, as well as emphasising the need for communication within the squad Haircuts are banned from taking place at the team hotel, with players expected to take care of these kinds of things before arriving on international duty Family visits will be heavily restricted during major tournaments, unlike the relaxed approach under Julian Nagelsmann. This is Klopp putting his mark on this team from day one, before a ball has even been kicked, setting the high standards that he was known for at Liverpool. It's clear that he wants complete focus on the footballing side of things with minimal outside influence, and for players to take the responsibility of representing their nation seriously. 												Published: 09/23/2026 BOGOTA, COLOMBIA, SEPTEMBER 23, 2026 ― Music Supervisor, Composer, and Mixing Engineer Santiago Uribe has built a career around producing music for film and television, contributing to more than 40 projects for Netflix, Amazon, Disney, HBO, and other international and local productions throughout Latin America and Spain. Uribe develops music for film and television, from composition and production to final mixing, using KRK V Series Studio Monitors as a trusted secondary reference throughout the process. Uribe’s path into music supervision began as streaming production expanded in Colombia and Latin America. After studying music production and engineering at Berklee College of Music in Boston, he returned to Colombia in 2010 to open Audiobit Studios, where he initially produced bands and composed music for television. In 2017, Netflix began producing more series in the region and local production companies started looking for music supervisors. Given his background, Uribe was among the few in the region who could jump into the role, and the opportunity quickly expanded to multiple platforms and countries. Today, he continues to balance music supervision with his composition, production, and mixing work, though his relationship with KRK predates that career evolution. While at Berklee, Uribe worked with KRK ROKIT monitors, establishing an appreciation for the brand’s sound that has continued throughout his life. “I did most of my work in college on KRKs, so when Enrique [Ferrer, Gibson CI Consultant] sent me the KRK V Series, I was pretty happy; it was like going back to my roots,” says Uribe. “I’ve always liked the sound profile and the tuning of the brand, and I’m excited to see (and listen to) what’s coming next from KRK.” Today, Uribe uses his KRK V Series monitors alongside a larger pair of boutique full-range speakers. The V Series provides an important perspective, helping him evaluate how his mixes translate to more typical listening environments. “The KRKs are amazing for reference,” he adds. “The monitors are great for when I want a second point of view on what I’m doing. They give me a different perspective on the mix, as well as how it would sound in a real-world application. They’re also great for checking how things will translate on smaller setups.” That translation is particularly important in Uribe’s work for film and television, where productions might contain substantial low-frequency information. This includes deep bass, drones, and other low-frequency sound design elements that will not necessarily translate to the consumer systems on which most audiences typically hear the finished production, such as televisions, laptops, or other consumer playback systems. Since he uses the KRKs without a subwoofer, Uribe says his setup provides a useful reality check. “I’m always verifying on the KRKs,” he continues. “The speakers provide a more realistic reference of the ways people are going to listen with a typical home setup, which doesn’t have extended low end.” Uribe also points to the midrange of the V Series monitors as a key advantage in his workflow. He notes that many speakers emphasize the extremes of the frequency spectrum, while the KRK V Series provides an important part of the spectrum for evaluating information through a mix. “Most speakers have this tuning range that’s sort of smiley face-shaped, with lots of bass and high-end, but the V-Series monitors have a flatter response and a detailed midrange, and that’s where most of the information is. It’s very important that we can hear those frequencies well.” For Uribe, the ability to move between large full-range monitors and the V Series is ultimately about making confident creative and technical decisions. “My other speakers are full-range, so I can hear very low frequencies on those,” he explains. “But nobody’s going to listen to those frequencies when they’re watching their TV. So, I’ve got to make sure it translates well.” As both a composer and mixing engineer, Uribe approaches those stages as a continuous process. Rather than separating composition from mixing, he develops the sonic character of a piece as he creates it. “When I’m recording or composing, I’m mixing,” he adds. “That way, when I finish the piece, it’s already mixed. I do it all at the same time.” That approach has supported a diverse body of screen work. Uribe has served as music supervisor and composer on the Netflix series “La Primera Vez” (known in English as “Eva Lasting”), creating the show’s original theme and developing new versions with artists like Manuel Medrano, Juliana, and Colombian salsa legends Grupo Niche, as well as Canadian duo Chromeo. The show’s evolving theme song became part of the audience experience, with viewers following along to see which artist would appear in each season. He also served as music supervisor and composer on the Netflix series “Medusa,” which became a major international success, and composed music for Amazon Prime Video’s “Los Billis.” Among Uribe’s current projects is a Spanish-language Netflix production, “En diciembre llegaban las brisas,” for which he is serving as music supervisor, composer, and music producer. Currently in production, the film’s music takes an ambitious creative approach inspired by its period setting and historical interpretations of more well-known modern songs. Uribe has also called on the KRK V Series for his work on this production. Uribe’s work has earned recognition in Colombia, with five Catalina Awards nominations and two Nuestra Tierra Awards wins for his “La Primera Vez” theme songs. With the Latin GRAMMY Awards now incorporating a “Best Music for Audiovisual” category, he also plans to submit his tv/film work to the Recording Academy for consideration. © 2026 MIX is part of Future plc, an international media group and leading digital publisher. title: Montgomery Named 2026 William V. Campbell Trophy Semifinalist - Iowa Hawkeyes Athletics
content: Fifth-year linebacker Jayden Montgomery has been named a finalist for the 2026 William V. Campbell Trophy, the nation’s premier scholar-athlete award. IOWA CITY, Iowa -- University of Iowa fifth-year linebacker Jayden Montgomery has been named a semifinalist for the William V. Campbell Trophy, it was announced Tuesday by the National Football Foundation. The honor is awarded annually to the nation’s top scholar athlete. As a finalist, he is also a member of the NFF National Scholar-Athlete Class and will receive an $18,000 postgraduate scholarship. Graves is one of 16 finalists for the award from a pool of 180 candidates nationwide. The winner of the Campbell Trophy will be announced Dec. 9, at the 67th NFF Annual Awards Dinner at the Bellagio Resort & Casino in Las Vegas. Montgomery (5-foot-11, 227) has captained an Iowa defense that is leading the nation scoring defense (4.3), total defense (176.7) and first down defense (25) through the first three weeks of the 2026 season. He was a Big Ten Distinguished Scholar in 2024 and 2025, and was recognized on the CSC Academic All-District Team in 2025. Former Hawkeye linebacker Jack Campbell was the first Iowa student-athlete to earn the William V. Campbell Trophy in 2022. Six previous players were named a NFF National Scholar Athlete, including defensive tackle Aaron Graves (2025), linebacker James Morris (2013), linebacker Mike Klinkenborg (2007), offensive lineman Derek Rose (1998, tight end Mike Flagg (1987), defensive back Bob Elliott (1975) and defensive lineman John Charles Hendricks (1968). title: Jack Dempsey v Gene Tunney at 100: when a great champion met his greatest inquisitor - The Guardian
content: On 23 September 1926, two of the best heavyweights in American history met in front of 120,000 fans in Philadelphia. The fight drew in a nation The two fights between Jack Dempsey and Gene Tunney rank with boxing’s most-storied championship bouts and are among the greatest sports spectacles ever seen in America. Wednesday marks the one hundredth anniversary of their first encounter. Dempsey bridged boxing’s old and modern eras and was one of the most charismatic fighters in history. When Dempsey was young, biographer Randy Roberts recounts, “he lived in mining camps and hobo jungles, rode the rods, and more than once begged for food. What separated him was his willingness, even eagerness, to work. He accepted any type of employment from washing dishes, cutting lawns, and scrubbing floors to the harder work of coal-mining, digging ditches, and picking fruit.” Dempsey had his own thoughts on his origin story: “I was a hobo,” Dempsey said. “But I was never a bum.” Fighting under the name “Kid Blackie”, Dempsey had roughly 100 fights in Colorado, Utah, and Nevada from 1911, when he turned 16, through 1914. “When you’re fighting, you’re fighting for one thing,” he later recalled. “To get money. When I was a young fellow, I was knocked down plenty. I wanted to stay down. I couldn’t. I had to collect that $2 for winning or go hungry. I had one fight when I was knocked down 11 times before I got up to win. I had to get up. I was a hungry fighter. When you haven’t eaten for two days, you’ll understand.” In the ring, Dempsey attacked with unrelenting ferocity. Trainer Ray Arcel likened him to “a saloon fighter” and observed, “With Dempsey, every part of your body was a legal target.” Sportswriter Paul Gallico echoed that theme, writing, “Dempsey seemed to have a constant bottomless well of cold fury somewhere close to his throat. He had tremendous courage, speed and determination, and good hitting powers. He was never a good boxer and had little or no defense. His protection was aggression. Dempsey never boxed anybody. When the bell rang, he ran out and began to attack his opponent, and he never stopped attacking him, trying to batter him to the floor until the bell ended the round. He had a smoldering truculence on his face and hatred in his eyes. He was utterly without mercy or pity, asked no quarter, gave none.” Dempsey said: “To be a good fighter, you have to have three things. You’ve got to be able to give it. You’ve got to be able to take it. And you’ve got to have a fighting heart.” Boxing was at low tide as America neared the “Roaring Twenties”. There hadn’t been a popular heavyweight champion since James Jeffries retired in 1904. Moral “reformers” were attacking the sport as sinful. And their efforts to abolish boxing gathered steam after Jack Johnson emerged as champion in 1908. On 5 April 1915, Jess Willard defeated Johnson in Havana. The new champion was poised for stardom. But after winning the title, Willard went on tour with Buffalo Bill’s Wild West Show and other theatrical companies, and defended his title only once in four years. Finally, in 1919, Tex Rickard, America’s premier boxing promoter, lured Willard back to the ring with a $100,000 guarantee to fight Dempsey in Toledo, Ohio on 4 July. It was the first major outdoor prizefight in the United States since Jeffries had come out of retirement and been battered into submission by Johnson on 4 July 1910. Willard weighed 245 lbs; Dempsey just 187. After three rounds, Willard’s jaw and nose were broken. Six teeth had been knocked out. There were cuts above and below his eyes. He could fight no more. Jack Dempsey was heavyweight champion of the world. Rickard wanted to make boxing a respectable sport that appealed to all classes. Dempsey’s exciting fighting style and charisma made him an ideal instrument to achieve that goal. Meanwhile, more and more states were legalizing boxing, and religious reform movements had begun to weaken. Dempsey versus Georges Carpentier followed and brought the sweet science to new heights. Dempsey-Carpentier was contested on 2 July 1921, in a temporary arena at Boyle’s Thirty Acres on the outskirts of Jersey City. More than 80,000 spectators (the largest crowd to witness a sporting event in America up until that time) attended. The live gate was $1,789,238 (more than double the previous record for a fight and equivalent to more than $32.5m today). The fight was also the first world championship bout to be broadcast live on radio, blow-by-blow. Carpentier was hailed as a man of destiny, not just in his French homeland but throughout Europe. He was the reigning world light-heavyweight champion. But more important to his image, he’d served in the military as a pilot during the first world war and been decorated twice for heroism. He was handsome, graceful, intelligent, debonair, spoke reasonably good English, and was regarded by many as the most glamorous fighter ever to step into a boxing ring. Dempsey was viewed as Carpentier’s opposite. He’d been indicted and tried (although acquitted) of fraudulently evading the draft during war. “He was dark complexioned,” Roberts notes. “His beard was coarse; his eyebrows were thick; and his face seemed cast in a permanent iron scowl. In the latter part of his career, Dempsey’s reserve in public would be recognized for what it was; basic shyness. But in 1921, his reserve and awkwardness around people were interpreted as the characteristics of a mean conceited man.” In other words, Dempsey-Carpentier was hero versus villain with the foreigner in the preferred role. “The Frenchman was the hero,” Dempsey later said. “I was the flat-nosed bum.” “The Fight of the Century” captured attention worldwide. On the morning of the bout, legendary sportswriter Grantland Rice wrote, “The greatest single day in the ancient history of an ancient sport has come at last; a day that has caught the imagination of more people from crowded centers to remote off-lying places than any single contest since the world’s dim dawn.” Vanderbilts, Rockefellers, Whitneys, and Astors were seated at ringside. The United States Senate and House of Representatives had adjourned in anticipation of the event because 12 senators and 90 congressmen had tickets. The fight was also attended by a significant number of women. Ladies had been present at Willard-Dempsey but were confined to a special section. At Dempsey-Carpentier, they mingled freely with the men. As was the custom of the day, the champion was introduced first. Dempsey later recalled, “Joe Humphreys picked up his megaphone and bawled, ‘In this corner, weighing 188lbs, from Salt Lake City, Utah, the heavyweight champion of the world, Jack Dempsey.’ The only response from 80,000 Americans was a little applause and a low murmur. ‘And in this corner, weighing 172lbs, the challenger from Paris, France, Georges Carpentier.’ The people went wild. It was deafening. It hurt; believe me.” The bell for round one rang at 3.16pm. At 3.30, it was over. “Carpentier had more charm, more good manners, and more class in his dress than anybody I had ever met,” Dempsey said years later. “But it was probably the worst mismatch in the history of the heavyweight division.” The New York Times devoted multiple pages to the fight and announced the result with a large-type, three-line headline that ran the full width of page one. “I read the stories about the fight in the next day’s papers,” Dempsey said later. “Carpentier was the hero of the hour. Never before had anybody seen such courage. I was just a butcher who happened to win. I was a pretty bitter fellow. No matter what you’ve got, you want them to like you.” Dempsey v Luis Firpo – Argentina’s “Wild Bull of The Pampas” – was the next building block for the Dempsey legend. On 14 September 1923, more than 88,000 fans filled the Polo Grounds in New York. An estimated 35,000 more were turned away. Once again, America’s blue-blood aristocracy was at ringside, joined this time by Babe Ruth. Ten seconds into round one, a left uppercut from Firpo dropped Dempsey to his knees. The champion rose and floored Firpo seven times. Then Firpo launched a series of blows punctuated by a monstrous right hand that knocked Dempsey out of the ring. That moment, recreated on canvas by artist George Bellows, is one of the most famous sports images of all time. Dempsey landed in the press section; cut his lower back on a typewriter; and with the aid of one or more writers, was pushed back into the ring before the count of 10. “It was pitch dark for a few seconds,” he said later. “Then I managed to focus on Firpo’s fuzzy form. I don’t remember climbing back in the ring, but I remember seeing 20 Firpos standing in front of me.” In round two, Dempsey knocked Firpo down twice more. The Argentinian was counted out at 57 seconds of the round. Then, like Willard before him, Dempsey put the title on ice, refusing to fight for three years. Finally, on 23 September 1926, he returned to the ring against Gene Tunney. Tunney was a brilliant tactician. The only defeat in his 67-bout career was a loss by decision to the great Harry Greb, who he fought five times. As a young man, Tunney had knocked out Soldier Jones on the undercard of Dempsey v Carpentier. Then, instead of going to his dressing room, he’d stayed at ringside and, still in his robe, watched the main event. Over the years, he’d studied films of Dempsey countless times. Tunney was complicated. He hadn’t graduated from high school but read prolifically as a road to self-improvement. That led to ridicule by some members of the press who treated his interest in books as a joke. During the build-up to Dempsey-Tunney, Paul Gallico wrote, “I think Tunney has hurt his own game with his cultural nonsense. It is a fine thing that he has educated himself to the point where he no longer says ‘dese’ and ‘dem’ and ‘dose’ and where he can tell one book from another and indicate some familiarity with their contents. But the man who steps into the ring with Dempsey with nothing but his hands as weapons needs to be a fighter and nothing but. He will have to have a natural viciousness and nastiness well up in him that will transcend rules and reason, that will make him want to commit murder with his two hands. I don’t think that Master Tunney, who likes first editions and works of art, has it in him.” That earned a rejoinder from Tunney, who declared, “It never occurred to me that a habit of reading could be seen as a stunt or a joke. Wasn’t reading something we wanted to champion?” A staggering total of 120,757 fans jammed Sesquicentennial Stadium in Philadelphia to witness Tunney challenge Dempsey for the heavyweight crown. That number and the $1,895,733 they paid in gate receipts (more than $36m in today’s dollars) were records for the time. An estimated 39 million more people listened to the fight on radio. The bout was scheduled for 10 rounds; a distance approved by both the champion, who was giving away youth, and the challenger, who thought that 10 rounds with Dempsey would be enough. At 29, Tunney was only two years younger than the champion. But Dempsey had lived a hard life. His body had absorbed the blows of hundreds of fights. And he’d been out of the ring for three years. It was a classic confrontation between a puncher who was past his prime and a boxer who was in it. “From the time the bout started,” Dempsey acknowledged later, “I was aware that my body and brain weren’t communicating properly. I was slower than I thought, or Gene was faster. He glided around the ring like he was on ice. Wherever I went looking for him, he stuck that left of his in my face, keeping me off balance, piling up points. Now and then, he’d stop me with a stiff right. There seemed to be nothing I could do, though I tried. Tunney was so scientific a boxer that all I seemed to be able to do was to take his punishment.” Tunney won every round. He cut Dempsey over the right eye and jabbed his left eye shut. By the end of the bout, the champion’s jaw was swollen and he was bleeding from the mouth. “I have no alibis to offer,” Dempsey said. “I lost to a good man.” Years later, he reflected back on that night and noted, “It’s sad to hear the fellow with the microphone yell: ‘The winner and new heavyweight champion of the world’ when you’re the old one.” But there was another memory of that day that the fallen champion carried with him. Late in life, he reminisced, “I was booed when I fought Willard, though he seemed twice my size. I fought a Frenchman before an American audience and was booed. I fought an Argentinian before my countrymen, and I was booed. It always dug deep and hurt terribly. But when I started to leave the ring [after losing to Tunney], something happened that had never happened to me before. To my surprise, I was loudly cheered; more than I had ever been cheered before. The people were cheering for me, clapping for me, calling out my name. I never realized how much I had hungered for a sound like that.” One year later, Dempsey and Tunney fought again. Tunney-Dempsey II unfolded before 104,843 fans at Soldiers Field in Chicago and generated boxing’s first $2m gate (the total was $2.7m). That encounter, which Tunney also won by decision, is best remembered for the “long count” controversy when referee Dave Barry refused to start counting until Dempsey went to a neutral corner after knocking Tunney down in round seven (the only time in Tunney’s career that he was on the canvas). title: One Pastor’s Perspective: Perfection v. Presence - Escondido Times-Advocate
content:
I would venture to guess that most of us desire to show up in the world with the right outfit, the curated home, and the perfect words for whatever occasion is before us. I often want nothing more than to walk into a room and just fit in, not over or under dressed, not too loud so as to draw attention, nor too quiet to be forgotten on the outskirts of conversation. While “perfect” might secretly be the goal, I will happily settle for “pretty good.” What I never want to be seen as is, “well, at least she tried.” As a pastor who stands up and preaches nearly every week, I want to not only do good, but be seen as good. The human longing to be accepted and thought of as capable is powerful. Beyond our own self-imposed standards, society often holds pastors to a distinct moral line. We expect that those who take on this calling do so with weight and care. There is an ancient Christian tradition, in persona Christi, meaning, “in the person of Christ,” which views ministers as acting as the physical representation of Christ when administering the sacraments. In those moments, the pastor serves as a conduit of grace to the congregation. They represent the divine in that moment. It is a high standard. Yet without realizing it, we sometimes extend that expectation of perfection to everything else—including physical appearance. (Once, after wearing a sleeveless dress on a 100-degree Sunday, a woman in a tank top told me I really should have worn a sweater to cover my arms.) Most of us simply want to be known or seen as competent, prepared and put-together. On most days, we probably are. But we are still far from flawless. Ironically, the places where we feel the deepest sense of belonging are the very places that never asked us to be perfect in the first place. Think for a moment about the people and spaces where you feel most at home. Do they care what you are wearing or whether you say the exact right thing every time? Likely not. Do they care about your presence, your honesty, and your love for them? Absolutely. Last week in worship, I realized that I was going to completely lose my composure and cry in front of my congregation (at least one of my worshiping congregations). I had finished preaching, we had sung, we had prayed and we were moving into the celebration of Communion. I began with the invitation I always give: “You’re invited to a meal that transcends time, a gathering rooted in God’s expansive embrace.” Then, right there before everyone, the tears came and I could not hold them back. I couldn’t continue. I had to pause, take a deep breath and remember that I am a human being – not expected to be flawless or perfect, just expected to be there and present. It turns out that God does not demand perfection – not in our daily living, not in our worship, in our generosity, nor in our ability to forgive. God simply asks for our presence. God asks that we show up to our lives, to our relationships, and to our faith – imperfect, honest, and willing to keep trying. After my very un-polished moment at the Communion table, I was reminded of this truth: neither God, nor people of God, need our performance. They just need us to show up – with a genuine desire to be known, seen and loved as we are. I hope that no matter what you may be going through or carrying in this time of life, you give yourself permission to be fully human. The Apostle Paul reminds us in 2 Corinthians 12:9, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” God isn’t waiting for the polished, flawless version of you to show up. You don’t need the perfect words, our outfit, or composure. Take a deep breath and remember that your presence is enough. Lisa Petty holds a Master of Divinity degree from the Iliff School of Theology and serves as the Lead Pastor of the First United Methodist Church, Escondido, located at 341 S. Kalmia St., in Escondido. Alongside Pastor Todd Stall and Pastor Ruben Torres, Rev. Lisa Petty leads worship Sunday mornings for Sanctuary Worship at 9  a.m., RISE Worship at 10:30 a.m., and Manantial Worship at 12:15 a.m. More information on First United Methodist Church, Escondido can be found at: www.fumcescondido.org Our Hometown
